turns.prompt_text: I've already built one deep in one medium using a 12 inch and an 8-in? Or maybe it was a 10-in board? So when I purchase these from Menards I need to cut them because 12 ft will not fit in my car I wonder could I just cleanly cut them in half?
turns.response_html:
Breaking a 12-foot board down into two 6-foot sections is usually the absolute easiest way to get lumber home in a standard car, but for hive boxes, cutting them exactly in half creates a serious headache at the workbench.

Here is the problem: a standard Langstroth box requires two sides (19.875 inches each) and two ends (16.25 inches each).

If you cut a 144-inch board perfectly in half into two 72-inch pieces, look at what happens when you try to cut your final pieces:

  • Piece 1 (72 inches): You cut two long sides ($19.875 \times 2 = 39.75\text{ inches}$). You have $32.25\text{ inches}$ left on this board. That is enough space to cut one end piece ($16.25\text{ inches}$), leaving you with a $16\text{-inch}$ scrap piece. Because a box end needs to be $16.25\text{ inches}$, you are short by a frustrating quarter of an inch, rendering that leftover scrap useless for this box.
  • Piece 2 (72 inches): You run into the exact same issue trying to match up the remaining ends and sides.

By letting the blade hit the dead center of the 12-foot board, you accidentally chop right through the middle of what should have been a clean, continuous run of box components, forcing a massive drop in efficiency.

The Solution: The "Asymmetrical Car Cut"

Instead of cutting them exactly at the 6-foot mark (72 inches), you can use the store's saw station to make a single, intentional offset cut. This lets the boards slide easily into your vehicle while keeping your math completely intact.

For a 3-Plank or 6-Plank Run: The 5-Foot / 7-Foot Split

Measure and cut your planks into one 5-foot section (60 inches) and one 7-foot section (84 inches).

  • The 5-Foot Board (60"): Yields exactly 3 End Pieces ($16.25 \times 3 = 48.75\text{ inches}$).
  • The 7-Foot Board (84"): Yields exactly 4 Side Pieces ($19.875 \times 4 = 79.5\text{ inches}$).

For a 5-Plank Run: The 6.5-Foot Split

Measure and cut your planks at 77 inches and 67 inches.

  • This specific split preserves the exact layout needed to net 8 total boxes from 5 planks with almost zero linear waste left over at the end of the project.

🛠️ A Quick Tip for the Store

Most big-box stores like Menards have a free hand-saw cutting station in the back lumber yard, or a powered radial arm saw up front. Since you just need these broken down to fit in the vehicle, you don't need to be microscopically precise down to the sixteenth of an inch in the store aisle—just ensure you leave an extra inch or two of breathing room on the longer side of your mark so you can square up the ends perfectly on your table saw at home!

turns.prompt_text: Okay so for a 5 plank I'm cutting six and a half cuts Is this for both the mediums and the deeps
turns.response_html:
Yes, this split works perfectly for both the deeps (12-inch boards) and the mediums (8-inch boards). Because a standard Langstroth deep and medium box use the exact same length and width footprint—meaning they both require the same 19.875-inch sides and 16.25-inch ends—their linear layout down the length of a 12-foot board is completely identical.

To clarify the exact measurement for the store: you will want to make a single cut on each board to split it into a 6.5-foot section (78 inches) and a 5.5-foot section (66 inches).

Here is exactly how those pieces break down on your workbench for both your 8-inch and 12-inch boards to yield 8 complete boxes from 5 planks:

  • From three of your planks:
    • The 78-inch section yields 3 side pieces ($19.875\text{ in} \times 3 = 59.625\text{ in}$).
    • The 66-inch section yields 4 end pieces ($16.25\text{ in} \times 4 = 65\text{ in}$).
  • From the remaining two planks:
    • The 78-inch section yields 3 side pieces and 1 end piece ($19.875\text{ in} \times 3 + 16.25\text{ in} = 75.875\text{ in}$).
    • The 66-inch section yields 1 side piece and 2 end pieces ($19.875\text{ in} + 16.25\text{ in} \times 2 = 52.375\text{ in}$).

When you add up all the pieces from those 5 planks, you get exactly 16 sides and 16 ends, giving you 8 perfect boxes with almost no wood wasted. Just measure out 78 inches at the Menards cutting station, make your single cut per board, and both your 8-inch and 12-inch planks will fit in the car while keeping your assembly line perfectly optimized!

turns.response_html:
Evaluating your manual input alongside finishing supplies helps clarify the exact economics of DIY vs. big-box retail. Adding a $28.00 can of linseed oil to the project changes your raw math, but analyzing the breakdown reveals if your manual labor truly beats the economy of scale.

1. The Cost of Finish Materials

A single standard quart or half-gallon can of linseed oil for $28.00 will easily coat 16 to 20 boxes depending on how heavily you apply it.

If you distribute that $28.00 finish expense across the 5 of each (16 total boxes) build, the finish adds $1.75 per box.

Your New DIY Total Cost Per Box (Wood + Linseed Oil Finish):

  • Deep Boxes: $13.75 (Lumber) + $1.75 (Finish) = $15.50 each
  • Medium Boxes: $8.75 (Lumber) + $1.75 (Finish) = $10.50 each

2. The Big-Box Beekeeping Retail Comparison

Unassembled commercial boxes from major players like Mann Lake or Dadant retail in specific price tiers based on quality grade:

  • Commercial/Select Grade (Few/no knots): Unassembled deeps run about $24.00 to $26.00 each. Medium supers run about $22.00.
  • Budget/Economy Grade (Tight knots allowed): Unassembled deeps run $20.95 to $21.99. Mediums run $16.95 to $18.99.
  • Shipping & Finish Tax: These commercial prices are for raw, unfinished wood. You still have to pay freight/shipping fees on heavy boxes, or buy your own paint/oil to finish them anyway.
Box TypeCommercial Retail (Raw + Shipped)Your Fully Finished DIY CostYour Direct Savings
Deep Box$21.00 – $25.00$15.50Save $5.50 – $9.50 per box
Medium Box$17.00 – $22.00$10.50Save $6.50 – $11.50 per box

3. Does the Economy of Scale Beat You?

Large beekeeping supply companies buy entire timber tracts and operate automated milling lines, which is why they can sell box kits relatively cheaply. However, they do not beat your localized DIY costs, for a few key reasons:

  1. Shipping Penalties: Wood is incredibly heavy. Commercial operations lose a massive portion of their scale efficiency to shipping and logistics when sending heavy boxes across the country. By driving to Menards and hauling the wood yourself, you pocket that entire logistical margin.
  2. Premium Material for Budget Price: Commercial "Budget Grade" boxes are often riddled with structural knots, minor cracks, or warped finger joints that require wood filler or filing during assembly. By picking out clear, clean #2 premium white pine boards yourself from the lumber stack, you are effectively building Select-grade quality boxes for significantly less than a commercial Budget-grade price.
  3. The Labor Valuation:
    • The Big-Box Kit Reality: When you buy a commercial "unassembled" box, you still have to spend time gluing it, squaring it, hammering or stapling the joints together, and painting or oiling the exterior.
    • The DIY Addition: Building from scratch only adds two steps to your workflow: making the straight cross-cuts to size and milling out the simple rebate/rabbet joints for the corners and frame rests.

Financial Conclusion

Your labor absolutely beats commercial scale here. Building a 5-and-5 run saves you roughly $120 to $160 in cash over purchasing online, leaves you with highly durable clear-pine boxes, and supplies you with a remaining $10.5\text{-foot}$ plank of clean wood that can be turned into free bottom boards and telescoping outer covers.
